content.text: Friction and drag are resistive forces that oppose motion. While often seen as problematic, these forces are essential for walking, driving, and many everyday activities. Understanding how they work helps us control and use them effectively.
Friction and drag are both resistive forces that oppose motion. Friction acts between solid surfaces in contact; drag acts on objects moving through fluids (liquids or gases, including air).
is the force that opposes the sliding or attempted sliding of two surfaces in contact.

Drag force increases with speed. This is why objects falling through air eventually reach a constant speed called terminal velocity -- the point where drag equals weight.

c) No, because there is still a resultant force and acceleration.
Friction between shoes and ground propels us forward
Friction between brake pads and discs slows vehicles
Friction allows us to hold objects
Friction is not always a 'bad' force. Without friction, you could not walk, drive, or hold objects. Friction between your shoes and the ground is what allows you to push off and move forward.
— Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces. Static friction can actually cause motion (e.g., when walking).
— Friction is (approximately) independent of contact area. A brick has the same friction lying flat or standing up.
— In air, yes (higher terminal velocity). In a vacuum, all objects fall at the same rate.
"Terminal velocity is the same for everyone"
— It depends on mass, area, and shape. A spread-eagled skydiver has lower terminal velocity than a diving one.
— Without friction, we couldn't walk, drive, or hold anything!
Static friction prevents motion; kinetic friction acts during sliding

Factors affecting friction: surface roughness, normal force
Factors affecting drag: speed, area, shape, fluid density
Friction can be beneficial (walking, braking) or harmful (wear, energy loss)
